newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bezeq using ISDN to fend off competition.
newsitem.headline: Bezeq using ISDN to fend off competition.

text.p: Bezeq Israel Telecom, participating in the launch on Sunday of a new telemedicine service, is looking for such innovative new applications to promote its new ISDN service.
Bezeq managing director Yitzhak Kaul said he sees ISDN as one of the key ways the company will face off new competition in basic telephone service by the end of the decade.

Telemedicine provides a platform for demonstrating ISDN, which was a key reason why Kaul attended the launching on Sunday of what he said was probably the world's first video-telephone service enabling home-bound patients to consult with a doctor.
The TV Phone service being offered by Shahal Medical Services of Tel Aviv uses a combination video-telephone to enable Shahal members to communicate with a physician by voice and picture.

"The advantage is it brings improved and earlier diagnosis," explained Yoram Alroy of Tel Aviv-based Shahal Medical Services. Shahal provides 40,000 subscribers with emergency medical services ranging from a medical databank to ambulance service.
"We have a lot of technology that is looking for an application," Kaul said. "Here we have a classic case of advanced technology used for the betterment of people."

ISDN, which stands for integrated services digital network, is an advanced digital communications line that can transmit for more information than conventional phone lines. Video is one application, but the most popular use is likely to be data transmission, particularly over the Internet.
Bezeq is just starting to introduce ISDN services in Israel and is looking for high-profile applications to catch the public's attention.

Bezeq is also providing ISDN lines to Tel Aviv's Beilinson hospital so that surgeons can communicate in real time with doctors in Jordan's King Hussein military hopsital and with doctors in Houston, Kaul said.
In the next several days, Bezeq ISDN lines will enable raidiologists to transmit medical images over phone lines between three Israeli hospitals, Kaul told Reuters.

Bezeq has just 2,000 ISDN lines installed to date, but Roni Haliva, manager for broadband services, hopes to instal another 20,000 to 25,000 this year. That pace, he said, should increase in the following years as ISDN demand grows.
"We see (ISDN) as a a substitute for regular telephone lines," said Haliva.

By mid-year all of the country's telephone exchanges should be able to handle ISDN and Haliva said in two to three months Israel will be the first country to adapt a single ISDN protocol, which will mark a breakthrough.
ISDN is crucial for Bezeq, which sees ISDN as a way to make its network competitive with cable television companies and other potential competitors in basic telephone service.
The Israeli government announced in December plans to open up basic phone service to competition after 1998, although it has not yet decided how it will do it.
